visits.text: The German Occupation Museum in Forest tells the story of the years when the German army occupied Guernsey, from June 30, 1940, to May 9, 1945, the day of liberation. It began in 1966 with the collection of an enthusiast, Richard Heaume. You can walk through a recreated street from the period. You can also see an Enigma machine, the device used to encrypt German messages. Arrive at 10 a.m.: the museum opens only in the morning, until 1 p.m., and accepts cash only.

visits.text: It crunches underfoot: Shell Beach, the “beach of shells,” lines Herm’s east coast. The sand is scattered with millions of tiny shell fragments, thought to be carried here by the Gulf Stream, the Atlantic’s great warm current. Allow around 20 minutes to walk from the harbor. A kiosk serves lunch during its operating season: check its dates before counting on it. There are no cars or bicycles on Herm: you get everywhere on foot.

Our favorite cove on Herm: Belvoir Bay, a small beach on the east coast. It is sheltered from the prevailing winds, so it feels warm in calm weather. Its clear water is inviting for a swim. Allow 15 minutes to walk from the harbor. The beach café operates during part of the warmer season: check its opening dates before you leave, and bring sunscreen.

St. Tugual’s Chapel stands in the heart of Herm’s small hamlet. It dates from the 11th century. Disciples of St. Tugual, a saint from Brittany, are thought to have settled on the site as early as the 6th century. Following restoration, the chapel reopened with a ceremony in May 2011. Step inside to see its stained-glass windows: Noah’s Ark appears alongside Guernsey cows, the island’s dairy breed.

Barely more than 2 km long, Herm still preserves traces of its earliest inhabitants. Chamber tombs survive on the Common, the large open area in the north of the island, and near the places known as Petit Monceau and Grand Monceau. These stone burial sites date from the Neolithic and Bronze Age and are several thousand years old. Cross the Common on your way to Shell Beach and follow the nature trail.

activities.text: Complete a circuit of Herm along its coastal paths: allow 2 hours at a leisurely pace. In the south, the cliff path connects Belvoir Bay to the top of the Rosaire Steps, the stairway where boats dock at low tide. On a clear day, the view stretches across the other islands and as far as France. In the north, seals frequent the rocks known as The Humps. In spring, watch for puffins, small seabirds with colorful beaks, resting on the water.

activities.text: In 1883, Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir spent a little over a month on Guernsey. He painted fifteen canvases there, almost all overlooking Moulin Huet Bay, a bay on the south coast. The Renoir Walk, a short trail through the valley, follows in his footsteps. Five empty frames, in the style of those he chose, stand where he worked: look through them to see his viewpoints. Bus 81 serves the site; wear good shoes for the path to the bay.

days_plan.itin_title: Guernsey and Sark in 3 Days: Hugo and Car-Free Islands

visits.text: A sheer drop to the left, a sheer drop to the right: La Coupée is the narrow ridge of land linking Great Sark to Little Sark, the southern part of the island. It stretches for 90 m, roughly 80 m above the sea, and is barely 3 m wide. Guardrails were not installed until 1900. The current road dates from 1945: German prisoners of war built it under the supervision of the Royal Engineers, the British Army’s engineering corps. Cross on foot and hold children by the hand.

La Seigneurie is the manor house of the Seigneur of Sark, a hereditary title. Until the electoral reform of 2008, the seigneur and landowners held a special place in the island’s institutions, inherited from its feudal system. The house dates from 1675. Its gardens are open to visitors from Easter through October. In the walled garden, cold-sensitive plants bloom from spring through fall, and a maze entertains children. Admission is £8 per adult; the house can only be visited on a guided group tour, by reservation.

Created to attract tourists, yet still striking: the Window in the Rock is an opening cut into the cliff on the west coast. It frames the rock arch at Port du Moulin and the Autlets rocks. It was commissioned by the Reverend William T. Collings, seigneur of the island from 1853, who wanted to develop its fledgling tourism industry. By the 1870s, Sark was already receiving around 5,000 visitors a year. You need to be sure-footed and comfortable with heights.

Two cells beneath a vaulted roof: that is the entirety of Sark’s prison, built in 1856. It was long considered the smallest working prison in the world. It no longer holds prisoners today. Under the judicial powers granted to the island in 1583, a prisoner could be held for no more than two days. In the center of the island, St Peter’s Church dates from 1820: landowning families partly funded it by purchasing their pews. Allow half an hour for both.

To reach the top of Sark, head up to Le Moulin, the old windmill standing at the island’s highest point, around 110 m above sea level. It was built in 1571, and its builder’s coat of arms is carved above the north door. In 1940, German troops removed its top to turn it into an observation post. Look up at the coat of arms before cycling away.

activities.text: From Herm, first return by boat to St Peter Port to catch the ferry to Sark: scheduled services do not connect the two islands directly. You will arrive at Maseline Harbour after a crossing of just under an hour from St Peter Port. Your bags, if clearly labeled, are delivered directly to your accommodations. Beyond the tunnel, the Tractor Bus, a passenger trailer pulled by a tractor, climbs steep Harbour Hill to the village; walkers take the footpath. On Sark, there are no cars: only tractors, bicycles, and horse-drawn carriages. Four bicycle rental businesses await you in the village.

The island’s most beautiful walk, in our view, starts on the other side of La Coupée, on Little Sark. Silver mines operated there in the 19th century, mainly at Port Gorey. In 1845, a tunnel collapse drowned ten miners. Burdened with debt, the Le Pelley family, who held the island, had to relinquish the fief, or seigneurie of Sark. The mine ruins are still visible at Port Gorey. Farther south, the Venus Pool, a natural pool among the rocks, appears only at low tide.

An inky sky above the fields: in January 2011, Sark became the world’s first “Dark Sky Island.” This designation from the International Dark-Sky Association recognizes places that protect their night skies from light pollution. In the evening, the observatory run by the Sark Astronomy Society, the island’s astronomy association, opens its sliding roof for guided sessions, by reservation. It is signposted from St Peter’s Church. Find the route during daylight: it crosses fields and is marked with reflective strips.

visits.text: Kitschy, perhaps, but touching: the Little Chapel is a miniature chapel covered in seashells, pebbles, and pieces of broken dishes. Brother Déodat, a member of a religious order, began it in March 1914 as a miniature replica of the grotto at Lourdes. He demolished his second version himself in 1923: the visiting Bishop of Portsmouth could not fit through the door. The current chapel measures 4.9 m by 2.7 m. Admission is free, with donations welcome, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. in winter and until 6 p.m. in summer. The steps are slippery in wet weather.

visits.text: Gray granite and sailboat masts just steps from the porch: the Town Church, St Peter Port’s parish church, stands beside the quays. A small chapel already occupied the site around 1020. The current church was consecrated in 1312. Its stair turret holds the oldest door in the Channel Islands. Look for a spaniel’s head carved into the granite: it was probably a stonemason’s signature.

“A rock of hospitality and freedom”: this is how Victor Hugo, exiled from France, describes Guernsey in the dedication to Toilers of the Sea. He bought Hauteville House in 1856 and lived there until 1870. He decorated it himself with chests, antique furniture, and earthenware in a medieval style. Les Misérables took shape in this house. On the top floor, the look-out, a small glass-enclosed room where he wrote, overlooks Herm and Sark. Visits are guided, last 1 hour, and require reservations: from April to early October, except Wednesdays.

On August 18, 1963, the Beatles played here in the former Candie Gardens pavilion, a venue since replaced by the museum. This public garden preserves two greenhouses from the late 18th century. The granite statue of Victor Hugo looks out over the harbor and sea: it was a gift from France in 1914. The garden also has a bronze statue of Queen Victoria. Admission is free, from dawn to dusk; from May to September, free concerts take place on Sundays at 3 p.m.

If Hugo has whetted your appetite, continue to the Guernsey Museum at Candie, the island’s museum, in the heart of the gardens. It displays the lintel—the stone placed above a doorway—from the haunted house described in Toilers of the Sea. The galleries tell the story of Guernsey’s earliest inhabitants and the island’s language. One section presents local legends, which fascinated the exiled writer. The museum opens daily, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. from late March to early November, then until 4 p.m.

An unusual ritual, and we love it: to climb Victoria Tower, you first need to borrow its key from the museum at Candie. Construction of this roughly 30-meter tower began in 1848. It commemorates Queen Victoria and Prince Albert’s visit in 1846. After 99 steps, the view stretches across the island’s west, north, and east coasts. Admission is free: the key is loaned for 30 minutes, with the last loan at 3:15 p.m.

activities.text: You will then head up High Street and the Pollet, St Peter Port’s pedestrian shopping streets. This is Guernsey’s only town, with around 19,000 residents. It is also the port where boats depart for Herm, Sark, Jersey, and England (Poole and Portsmouth). Take the opportunity to locate the kiosk selling tickets to Herm, near the Weighbridge on the harborfront.

If high tide falls late in the day, head down to La Vallette Bathing Pools, seawater swimming pools on St Peter Port’s waterfront. People have been swimming here sheltered from the waves since 1865. The sea fills them at every high tide, and their low walls retain some water as the tide recedes. Above them, Clarence Battery, a former gun emplacement built in 1780, offers a lovely view of the town and Castle Cornet, the harbor’s castle. Bring a swimsuit and towel.

You will take the ferry from Sark back to St Peter Port, a crossing of less than an hour, to catch your flight or boat. From the harbor, ferries serve Jersey and England (Poole and Portsmouth). Guernsey Airport is in the parish of Forest, southwest of town. Sark’s boat schedules change with the season: choose your flight to fit your return crossing.
